title: How to Grow a Podcast with Radical Authenticity | Ep 70
guestBio: Erin Washington is an author, motivational speaker, body image advocate, and host of the top 1% podcast ThERINpy. A former D1 athlete and mom of two, she is also the founder of the Blue Butterfly Foundation — a mentorship community for teen girls — and the author of From Pain to Purpose. She built her platform by sharing every step of her growth journey so other women feel seen and less alone.
excerpt: Erin Washington turned a pandemic Instagram Live series into a radio-produced podcast deal — and then grew it into a top 1% show by doing the one thing most people are too scared to try: being completely, unapologetically herself. In this episode, she hands over the full playbook — from booking Katie Couric to walking away from a trademarked brand — so you can stop performing and start building something that's actually yours.
metaDescription: Erin Washington reveals her authenticity-first strategy for growing a top 1% podcast — guest booking, branding, consistency, and finding your voice.
keyTakeaways: The thing you're most afraid to share is almost always the thing that's quietly holding your platform — and your life — back.
Your audience can't find you until you stop filtering who you are; authenticity isn't a strategy, it's the foundation everything else is built on.
Pitch the publicist, not the celebrity, and always lead with a compelling angle that serves their client's current narrative.
One high-profile guest creates the credibility chain that makes booking the next ten dramatically easier.
Judge your week, not your day — extending yourself the same grace you'd give a friend is a genuine growth strategy, especially for moms.
Talking openly about your wins doesn't make you arrogant; it teaches your kids that it's safe and good to shine.
When you feel called to pivot — whether that means rebranding, rebuilding, or starting over — leaning into that pull elevates everything around you.

quiz.title: What's Your Podcaster Personality?
quiz.description: Whether you're dreaming of hitting record for the first time or already deep in the game, the way you show up on a platform says everything about how you're wired to connect. Answer these six questions honestly — there are no wrong answers, only clearer mirrors. Find out which podcaster archetype lives inside you.

A.name: The Vault Keeper
A.description: You are sitting on a story that could change someone's life — and you know it. The reason you haven't shared it yet isn't laziness or lack of ambition; it's the quiet, persistent belief that vulnerability is a risk you can't afford. But here's what this episode will show you: the thing you've been protecting the most carefully is almost certainly your greatest asset. Erin Washington built a top 1% show by releasing exactly what she'd been guarding for years. This conversation is your permission slip.

B.name: The Strategic Builder
B.description: You are methodical, intentional, and allergic to wasted effort — which means you've probably spent more time planning your platform than actually building it. You want the roadmap before you take the first step, and honestly, that instinct has served you well in other areas of your life. This episode will give you the exact framework you've been waiting for: Erin's step-by-step guest-booking strategy, her branding pivot playbook, and Aimee's casting-session approach to interviews. Now you have no excuse not to start.

C.name: The Reluctant Rebel
C.description: You've been told to stay in your lane so many times that you've started to believe it — even though some part of you keeps drifting toward something bigger, louder, and more you. You're not afraid of hard work. You're afraid of standing out and being seen doing it. Erin Washington was a homecoming queen who hid her truth for years. She will show you what's waiting on the other side of that fear, and it is so much better than the lane you've been assigned.

D.name: The Momentum Maker
D.description: You are already in motion — building, creating, posting, recording — and you are not slowing down for anyone. What you sometimes miss, though, is the signal in the noise: the pivot that's calling you, the rebrand that's overdue, the one honest thing you keep editing out of every episode. This conversation between Aimee and Erin is a gut-check for women who are moving fast and need a moment to ask whether they're moving in the right direction — and whether they're bringing their real self along for the ride.

questions.question: When you imagine sharing something deeply personal online, your first instinct is:

options.text: Freeze — there are things I protect fiercely and I'm not sure I'm ready to let them go
Plan — I'd want to think through the angle, the timing, and the audience before posting anything
Shrink — I worry about what people will think or say, so I usually pull back
Post — I'd probably hit share before I talked myself out of it

questions.question: Your approach to building an audience is closest to:

options.text: Waiting until I have something truly meaningful to say before putting myself out there
Researching best practices and developing a clear strategy before I launch
Watching what others do and wondering if I could ever pull something like that off
Testing, iterating, and figuring it out in real time as I go

questions.question: When your life feels chaotic — a move, a breakup, a health scare — your creative output:

options.text: Goes quiet — I tend to go inward and process privately before I share anything
Gets more structured — I use planning and output as a way to feel in control
Stops almost entirely — I can't create when things feel unstable
Spikes — chaos tends to fuel me and give me the most raw material to work with

questions.question: If someone asked you why you haven't started your podcast yet, you'd most honestly say:

options.text: Because I'm not sure I'm ready to be that open — there's a lot I haven't said publicly
Because I want to have the right equipment, the right format, and the right strategy first
Because I don't think anyone would actually want to listen to me
I already have — or I'm just about to

questions.question: When you hear someone talk openly about their biggest win, you feel:

options.text: Inspired, but also a little guarded — I wouldn't feel comfortable doing the same thing
Curious about the process — I want to understand exactly how they got there
A complicated mix of admiration and something that looks a little like envy
Energized — I love celebrating wins and I want to do the same out loud

questions.question: The kind of content you're most naturally drawn to create is:

options.text: Deeply personal stories — when I do share, I want it to mean something real
Educational or strategic — I want to teach people something valuable and actionable
I'm honestly still figuring out what my thing is, and that uncertainty holds me back
Whatever feels alive right now — I follow my energy and my audience follows me

content:
There is a version of you that has something to say. You've felt her. She shows up right before you talk yourself out of hitting record, right before you decide your story isn't interesting enough, your voice isn't polished enough, your life isn't together enough. This episode is for her — and for you.

Erin Washington is the host of ThERINpy, a top 1% podcast, the founder of the Blue Butterfly Foundation, and the author of From Pain to Purpose. She is also, by her own admission, someone who spent years guarding a secret that she thought would disqualify her from being taken seriously. When she finally let it go — on the internet, in public, for anyone to hear — it didn't break her. It built her.

The Pandemic Pivot That Started Everything

Before there was a podcast, there were Instagram Lives. During the earliest days of the pandemic, Erin started showing up on Instagram not because she had a content strategy, but because she needed connection — and so did everyone else. Those raw, unscripted conversations caught the attention of the largest radio station in Washington, D.C., and before long she had a produced podcast deal. Not because she had a media kit. Not because she had a following that made brands nervous. Because she was real in a moment when everyone else was performing calm.

That origin story matters because it dismantles the myth that you need to have everything figured out before you start. Erin didn't wait until she had a studio. She didn't wait until she had a brand. She showed up, she spoke honestly, and the right people found her because of it.

The Secret That Freed Her — And Her Audience

Every platform has a turning point — a moment when the creator stops managing her image and starts telling the truth. For Erin, that moment came when she shared something she had kept private through homecoming crowns and D1 athletics and years of building a public life. She doesn't ask you to share everything. She asks you to notice what you're refusing to share — because that thing is usually the exact key that unlocks the door between you and your people.

This is something Aimee and Erin sit with together in this conversation: the cost of the curated self. The perfect grid. The highlight reel. Erin tried that approach. She describes watching her engagement flatline while she chased an aesthetic, and then watching everything shift the moment she let the mess be visible. Your audience is not looking for proof that you've arrived. They are looking for someone who makes them feel less alone in where they are.

The Guest-Booking Masterclass You Didn't Know You Needed

If you've ever wondered how independent podcasters land guests like Katie Couric, Melissa Joan Hart, and Gabby Bernstein — this is the section of the episode you'll want to replay. Erin did not buy a contact list. She did not DM celebrities in the hopes of going viral. She reverse-engineered the process by understanding one foundational truth: you don't pitch the celebrity, you pitch the publicist — and you pitch them an angle, not a favor.

Erin walks through her exact process: how she identifies what a public figure is promoting, how she crafts an angle that genuinely serves their client's current narrative, and how one well-placed yes creates the credibility that makes every subsequent booking easier. The Katie Couric booking, she reveals, came from a single detail she noticed in Couric's memoir that no one else was talking about. That kind of specificity — that proof that you've done the work — is what separates a request from an opportunity.

She and Aimee also get into their opposing philosophies on pre-calls, and it is genuinely one of the most useful debates you'll hear about podcast production. Erin skips them entirely, believing the best conversations happen when both people are discovering things in real time. Aimee runs hers like casting sessions, vetting for energy and alignment before a single mic goes live. Both approaches work. Both reflect deeply held values about what makes a great show. The question is which one is yours.

Rebranding, Pivoting, and the Gabby Bernstein Moment

Erin built a following under the name Squats & Margaritas. It was fun, it was catchy, and it was trademarked. It was also, eventually, too small for what she was becoming. The rebrand to ThERINpy wasn't just a name change — it was an act of alignment, a decision to let her platform grow into who she actually was rather than who she was when she started.

The catalyst, she shares, came from a conversation with Gabby Bernstein — a guest she'd spent months working to book — who said something so direct, so on point, that Erin knew the moment it landed that she couldn't unhear it. She doesn't frame the pivot as a loss. She frames it as the most important brand decision she ever made, because it was the first one she made entirely for herself.

Grace as a Strategy, Wins as a Practice

One of the quieter but more lasting threads in this conversation is what Erin and Aimee call judging your week, not your day. If you are a working mom, a creative, a woman building something in the margins of a full life, you know the particular cruelty of measuring yourself against a single bad afternoon. Erin's reframe — zoom out, give yourself the week, and evaluate from there — is not a productivity hack. It is a form of self-respect.

She also makes a point that lands hard: when you talk about your wins openly, you are not bragging. You are modeling. Your kids are watching you decide whether it is safe to be proud of yourself. They are learning, right now, what it looks like when a woman succeeds and what she does with that success. You celebrating yourself is not vanity. It is permission — for them, and for every woman watching who hasn't given it to herself yet.

You Don't Need to Be Ready. You Need to Be Real.

Erin Washington did not build a top 1% podcast by being the most polished person in the room. She built it by being the most present. By sharing the thing she was afraid to share. By pitching with specificity and receiving with grace. By choosing, again and again, to be recognizably herself even when the algorithm suggested otherwise.

If you have a story — and you do — this episode is your roadmap. Not to build Erin's show, but to build yours. Stop performing. Start building. Your people are already looking for you.
